Criminal Law Practice Guide

Arrest, Detention, and Judicial Remand (Thap Myad) in Nepalese Criminal Law

📅 Published: 2025-02-20
🔄 Updated: 2025-10-01
⏱ 9 min read
🔍 Review: Senior Advocate Lead Counsel, Supreme Court Bar Association
Direct Legal Answer & Overview

In Nepal, police can detain an individual for a maximum of 24 hours without court authorization. To hold an accused person longer for investigation, police must produce the detainee before the District Court and formally request Judicial Remand (Thap Myad / थप म्याद) under Section 14 of the Muluki Criminal Procedure Code 2074. The judge evaluates the investigation progress, conducts a physical health review, hears defense counsel, and decides whether to grant a limited remand extension (typically 3 to 7 days at a time).

Key Practical Takeaways

  • Strict 24-hour constitutional limit on unmonitored police custody.
  • Judicial remand hearings (Thap Myad) are held in open court before a District Judge.
  • Defense advocates can oppose remand extensions, request medical exams, and challenge arbitrary custody.

The transition from initial police arrest to formal court proceedings is a critical juncture where personal liberty is balanced against the state's duty to investigate crime. Under the Muluki Criminal Procedure Code 2074, judicial remand—known as Thap Myad (थप म्याद)—acts as a vital judicial check against arbitrary police detention.

1. The 24-Hour Constitutional Rule

Under Article 20(3) of the Constitution of Nepal, every arrested person must be physically presented before the competent judicial authority within 24 hours of arrest, excluding the time required for travel from the place of arrest to the court. If police fail to produce the accused within this window, the continued detention becomes unconstitutional, entitling the detainee to apply for a writ of Habeas Corpus (बन्दी प्रत्यक्षीकरण) before the High Court or Supreme Court.

2. How Judicial Remand (Thap Myad) Hearings Work

When police require additional time to interrogate suspects, inspect crime scenes, or await forensic lab reports, the Investigating Officer submits a written Remand Application to the District Court. During this hearing:

  • The District Judge directly asks the detainee if they were subjected to physical assault or torture in police custody;
  • The judge inspects the mandatory government hospital medical examination report;
  • The defense advocate argues why further custody is unnecessary, highlighting lack of evidence or requesting that questioning take place while the person remains at liberty; and
  • The court grants only such number of days as strictly justified by the factual progress of the investigation (usually 3 to 7 days per extension).

3. Statutory Limits on Maximum Police Custody

Police custody cannot continue indefinitely. Under Section 15 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the total cumulative period of remand cannot exceed 25 days for general offenses. In specialized offenses (such as organized crime or banking offenses), specific statutes prescribe maximum custody periods (e.g. up to 60 days in organized crime) before a formal charge-sheet must be filed or the accused released.

Statutory Citations & Governing Nepal Legislation

Statute / Act Section / Rule Legal Significance
Muluki Criminal Procedure Code 2074 Section 14 & 15 (Remand & Custody Timelines) Rules for judicial detention extensions and statutory investigation limits.
Constitution of Nepal 2072 Article 20(3) Mandatory production before judicial authority within 24 hours.

Documentary Checklist for this Procedure

  • ✔ Official Arrest Memo (Pakrau Purji)
  • ✔ Police Remand Extension Application (Thap Myad Nivedan)
  • ✔ Medical Examination Report issued prior to custody transfer

Frequently Asked Questions on this Topic

Can a defense advocate be present during Thap Myad hearings in Nepal?

Yes. The accused has a constitutional right to legal representation during all remand hearings. The advocate appears before the bench to oppose unnecessary remand extensions and request hospital treatment or release.
